proof.text: Work with formal symbols, not with chosen sets of objects or arrows of a dg category. Introduce $O$, the sorts $A_n$ for $n\in\mathbf Z$, and endpoint arrows $s_n,t_n$. Introduce the binary product vertex $B$ with projections $\pi_s,\pi_t$ and arrows $p_n:A_n\to B$, with relations $\pi_s p_n=s_n$ and $\pi_t p_n=t_n$. For each $n$ introduce a pullback vertex $P_n$ of $p_n$ with itself. For each $(q,p)$ introduce a pullback vertex $C_{q,p}$ of $s_q:A_q\to O$ and $t_p:A_p\to O$. In each case add the projections and the commuting-square relation. Mark these product and pullback cones as specified cones. These are finite diagrams; being specified does not assert that they are limits in the indexing category.

proof.text: Construct the additional variable contexts as finite products of copies of $O$ and $A_n$, followed by the endpoint equalities required for the relevant formula. Concretely, an equality $u=v$ of two endpoint expressions on a context $T$ is encoded by a pullback of $(u,v):T\to B$ along the diagonal $O\to B$, whose two projection composites are $1_O$. Restrict the variable projections to this pullback. Repeating this finite construction encodes every finite list of endpoint equalities. Mark its product and pullback cones and impose their cone commutativity relations. This gives parallel triples for module associativity, composable triples for composition associativity, and the mixed parallel/composable triples for bilinearity. No equalizer cone or infinite diagram is required.

source.place: Tabuada, Chapter 1, Definition 1.1 and section 1.3.1 preceding Lemma 1.10, printed pp. 25, 28-30; explicit sketch construction supplied by the agent, not asserted by Lemma 1.10.

proof.text: Add $z_n:B\to A_n$, unary negation $-_n$, unary multiplication $[r]_n$ for every $r\in R$, and $+_n:P_n\to A_n$. Impose $p_nz_n=1_B$, and require $p_n$ after a unary operation to equal $p_n$, and after addition to equal either common endpoint-pair map of $P_n$. Add $1:O\to A_0$ with $s_0 1=t_0 1=1_O$. Add $c_{q,p}:C_{q,p}\to A_{p+q}$ with source $s_p$ of the second factor and target $t_q$ of the first, and $d_n:A_n\to A_{n+1}$ with $s_{n+1}d_n=s_n$, $t_{n+1}d_n=t_n$. Thus the endpoints of every constructed expression are prescribed recursively.

source.place: Tabuada, Chapter 1, Definition 1.1 and section 1.3.1 preceding Lemma 1.10, printed pp. 25, 28-30; explicit sketch construction supplied by the agent, not asserted by Lemma 1.10.

proof.text: On each parallel-variable context impose $(a+b)+c=a+(b+c)$, $a+b=b+a$, $a+z_n(p_n a)=a$, $a+(-a)=z_n(p_n a)$, $1_Ra=a$, $(rs)a=r(sa)$, $(r+s)a=ra+sa$, and $r(a+b)=ra+rb$. Here all variables have degree $n$ and equal endpoint pairs; each displayed equality has target $A_n$. These are the abelian-group and unital $R$-module equations, expressed as parallel arrows. Impose composition associativity $(cb)a=c(ba)$ on composable triples of degrees $r,q,p$, with target $A_{p+q+r}$, and $1_{t(a)}a=a=a1_{s(a)}$ on $A_p$. Bilinearity is imposed on triples $(b,b^{\prime},a)$ and $(b,a,a^{\prime})$ by $(b+b^{\prime})a=ba+b^{\prime}a$, $b(a+a^{\prime})=ba+ba^{\prime}$, $(rb)a=r(ba)$ and $b(ra)=r(ba)$. The parallel pairs in the sums exist because step 3 gives identical endpoints.

source.place: Tabuada, Chapter 1, Definition 1.1 and section 1.3.1 preceding Lemma 1.10, printed pp. 25, 28-30; explicit sketch construction supplied by the agent, not asserted by Lemma 1.10.

proof.text: Impose $d(a+a^{\prime})=d(a)+d(a^{\prime})$, $d(ra)=r\,d(a)$, $d(z_n(x,y))=z_{n+1}(x,y)$ and $d(-a)=-d(a)$ on their finite contexts. Impose $d_0 1=z_1\Delta$ on $O$, where $\Delta:O\to B$ is the diagonal, and $d_{n+1}d_n=z_{n+2}p_n$ on $A_n$. On $C_{q,p}$ impose $d(ba)=d(b)a+(-1)^q b\,d(a)$. The two product terms belong to $A_{p+q+1}$: the first has degrees $(q+1,p)$, the second $(q,p+1)$; both have source $s_p(a)$ and target $t_q(b)$. Their sum is therefore defined on the parallel-pair vertex. Choose $(-1)^q$ to mean $1_R$ for even $q$ and $-1_R$ for odd $q$, including negative integers. Equal integer indices such as $p+(q+1)$ and $(p+q)+1$ designate the same sort, so every imposed relation has one source and one target.

proof.text: Make every tuple occurring in steps 1-5 an actual arrow of the presentation. If expressions $u_i:T\to X_i$ are used as a product tuple, add $\langle u_i\rangle:T\to P$ and relations $\pi_i\langle u_i\rangle=u_i$. For a pullback tuple $(u,v)$, use the same rule with its two projections, only when the required equality of their base composites has a finite derivation from the relations already imposed. The commuting-square relation and the projection equations then give a commuting cone. Start with variables and operation symbols; at each finite stage allow operation application, composition, these tuple constructors, and substitution into an already formed expression or equation. A term or a derivation is a finite tree, so induction on its height shows that the union of all finite stages contains every well-typed finite expression and its substitutions. No step asks for a limit in the free category: tuple arrows are generators with the stated projection relations.

proof.text: The above syntax is $\mathcal U$-small. Its labels lie in a set formed from $R$, $\mathbf Z$ and finitely many constructor labels, in the universe fixed by [def-weil-size-convention]. Contexts, expression trees, finite equality derivations and cone descriptions are encoded by finite strings of these labels with parentheses and variable indices in $\mathbf N$. At each fixed length they are a subset of a finite power of a $\mathcal U$-set; taking the union over $\mathbf N$ remains in $\mathcal U$. The well-typed ones are subsets of this set. In particular, closure under substitutions in step 6 adds no proper class of symbols or relations, and the set of specified cones is $\mathcal U$-small.

source.place: Tabuada, Chapter 1, Definition 1.1 and section 1.3.1 preceding Lemma 1.10, printed pp. 25, 28-30; explicit sketch construction supplied by the agent, not asserted by Lemma 1.10.

proof.text: Let $Q$ be the small graph with the constructed sorts as vertices and all operation arrows, projections and tuple arrows as edges. Form $P(Q)$ explicitly: its arrows are finite composable edge lists, its identities are empty lists, and composition concatenates lists. The category identities are the empty-list identities and associativity of concatenation. The arrows form a subset of the finite strings over the small edge set, so $P(Q)$ is $\mathcal U$-small by the same size bound as step 7. Let $r$ relate exactly the parallel paths prescribed equal in steps 1-6. Apply [lem-coef-category-quotient-relations] to $P(Q)$ and $r$. Its quotient is a small category with the same vertices and path classes as arrows, exactly the free category on the displayed generators modulo their equations. Write it as $S_R$.

source.place: Tabuada, Chapter 1, Definition 1.1 and section 1.3.1 preceding Lemma 1.10, printed pp. 25, 28-30; explicit sketch construction supplied by the agent, not asserted by Lemma 1.10.

proof.text: Pass all the marked finite cones to $S_R$ using the quotient functor; their commuting equations hold because they are among the imposed relations. Their indexing diagrams are still finite, regardless of identifications of arrows in the quotient. There is a small family of such cones by step 7. Hence $S_R$, with precisely these specified finite product and pullback cones, is a finite-limit sketch by the definition in [lem-coef-finite-limit-sketch-models]. That definition requires a model to take the specified cones to limits; it does not require all cones in $S_R$ to be limits or require the category $S_R$ itself to have finite limits. This establishes the claimed signature sketch and the tuple-arrow convention.

title: Finite-limit sketch signature for small R-linear dg categories
statement: Fix universes $\mathcal U\in\mathcal V$ as in [def-weil-size-convention] and a commutative ring $R\in\mathcal U$. A finite-limit sketch and its Set-valued models mean those of [lem-coef-finite-limit-sketch-models]. The following signature admits a $\mathcal U$-small indexing category and a $\mathcal U$-small family of specified finite product and pullback cones, defining a sketch $S_R$. Its primary sorts are $O$ and $A_n$ for every $n\in\mathbf Z$, with $s_n,t_n:A_n\to O$. It has the sort $B=O\times O$, the map $p_n=(s_n,t_n):A_n\to B$, the parallel-pair sorts $A_n\times_B A_n$, the composable-pair sorts $A_q\times_O A_p$ (where $s_q$ equals $t_p$), and the finite tuple sorts needed for the equations below. The operations are $z_n:B\to A_n$, negation and scalar multiplication by each $r\in R$ on $A_n$, addition on parallel pairs, $1:O\to A_0$, composition $c_{q,p}:A_q\times_O A_p\to A_{p+q}$, and $d_n:A_n\to A_{n+1}$. All preserve the appropriate endpoints; $p_nz_n=1_B$ and $s_0 1=t_0 1=1_O$. Relations impose the $R$-module equations in each fiber of $p_n$, associativity and two-sided units for composition, bilinearity of composition, linearity of $d$, and, on each appropriate tuple sort, $d(1)=0$, $d_{n+1}d_n=z_{n+2}p_n$, and $d(ba)=d(b)a+(-1)^q b\,d(a)$ for $b\in A_q$, $a\in A_p$. Each tuple-valued expression used in these equations is an arrow to the corresponding product or pullback vertex, with its composites with the projections prescribed by the expression; the same convention is closed under the substitutions of well-typed finite expressions. The indexing category is the free category on these sorts, operation and tuple arrows and cone projections modulo these equations. Only the stated finite product and pullback cones are required to be limit cones.
